essays.stem: Explain how engineering materials are grouped into ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals and non-metals. Give two examples of each group and a use for each example.
essays.modelAnswer: Ferrous metals contain mostly iron. Most are magnetic, and most rust if they are not protected. Examples are mild steel, used for gates, grills and frames, and cast iron, used for engine blocks and machine bases. Non-ferrous metals contain little or no iron, so they do not rust in the same way and most are not magnetic. Examples are aluminium, which is light and is used for window frames and ladders, and copper, which carries electricity and heat well and is used for wiring and water pipes. Brass and bronze are also non-ferrous. Non-metals include plastics, rubber, timber, ceramics and composites. Examples are PVC, used for water pipes and cable covers, and rubber, used for seals, hoses and tyres. Each group is chosen for the properties the job needs.
markingPoints: Ferrous: mostly iron, usually magnetic, rusts
Two ferrous examples with suitable uses
Non-ferrous: little or no iron, with two examples and uses
Non-metals: two examples with suitable uses
Links the choice of material to the properties the job needs

essays.stem: Describe low-carbon (mild), medium-carbon and high-carbon steel, and cast iron. For each, give the rough carbon content, its main properties and a typical use.
essays.modelAnswer: Low-carbon or mild steel has about 0.1–0.3% carbon. It is soft, ductile and easy to cut, bend and weld, so it is used for most fabrication work: gates, burglar bars, frames, brackets and sheet work. Medium-carbon steel has about 0.3–0.6% carbon. It is stronger and harder but less easy to bend and weld, and it is used for shafts, axles, gears and bolts. High-carbon steel has from about 0.6% to over 1% carbon. It can be made very hard, but it is more brittle and hard to weld, so it is used for tools such as chisels, springs, files and knives. Cast iron has about 2–4% carbon. It is hard and brittle and can crack if it is hit or bent, but it casts well into shapes and resists wear, so it is used for engine blocks, machine bases and pipe fittings.
markingPoints: Mild steel: about 0.1–0.3% carbon, soft, ductile, weldable, used for general fabrication
Medium-carbon steel: about 0.3–0.6%, stronger, used for shafts, axles, bolts
High-carbon steel: about 0.6% to over 1%, can be hardened, brittle, used for tools and springs
Cast iron: about 2–4%, hard and brittle, casts well, used for engine blocks and bases
States that more carbon gives a harder, less ductile steel that is harder to weld

essays.stem: Explain the difference between physical properties (such as density, melting point and conductivity) and mechanical properties (such as strength, hardness and toughness). Give two examples of each and say why a welder needs to know them.
essays.modelAnswer: Physical properties describe what a material is like without any force being put on it. Density is how heavy it is for its size: aluminium is about one third as dense as steel, so it is used where weight matters. Melting point is the temperature at which it turns to liquid: aluminium melts at about 660 °C, far below steel, so it needs less heat and can suddenly collapse. Conductivity is how well it carries heat or electricity: copper carries heat away fast, so it needs more heat to braze or weld. Mechanical properties describe how a material behaves under a load or force. Strength is how much load it can carry before it breaks, hardness is how well it resists scratching and wear, and toughness is how well it takes a sudden blow. A welder needs to know these to choose the right material, process, filler and heat, and to avoid cracking or melting the job.
markingPoints: Physical properties: what the material is like without a force on it
Two physical properties explained with correct examples
Mechanical properties: how the material behaves under a load or force
Two mechanical properties explained with correct examples
Explains why a welder needs them: choosing material, process and heat, avoiding cracking or melting

essays.stem: Describe four simple workshop tests used to identify an unknown metal, and what each test shows.
essays.modelAnswer: Appearance: look at the colour and surface. Copper is reddish, brass is yellow, aluminium is a light silver-grey, mild steel is dark grey with mill scale, and stainless steel is bright silver. Weight: lift the piece and compare it with steel of the same size; aluminium feels much lighter. Magnet test: a magnet sticks to iron and most steels, but not to aluminium, copper, brass or the stainless steel used for most sinks and rails, so it tells ferrous from non-ferrous metals. File test: try a file on a corner. If it cuts easily the metal is soft, like mild steel or aluminium; if it skids, the part is hardened. Spark test: touch a bare ferrous sample lightly on a grinder, wearing eye protection, and watch the sparks. Mild steel gives long, straw-coloured streamers with few bursts, high-carbon steel gives many bright bursts, and cast iron gives short, dull red sparks.
markingPoints: Appearance and colour, with correct examples
Weight compared with steel of the same size
Magnet test separates ferrous from non-ferrous (with the stainless steel exception)
File test shows soft or hardened material
Spark test on bare ferrous metal only, with eye protection, and what the sparks show

essays.stem: Compare aluminium and mild steel as materials for fabrication work. Think about weight, strength, corrosion, magnetism, melting and joining.
essays.modelAnswer: Aluminium is much lighter than mild steel, about one third of the weight for the same size, so it is used where weight matters, such as ladders, boat parts and window frames. Mild steel is stronger and stiffer for the same size, and cheaper, so it is used for gates, frames and structures. Mild steel rusts if it is not painted or galvanised, especially near the sea; aluminium forms a thin oxide layer that protects it, so it does not rust. A magnet sticks to mild steel but not to aluminium. Aluminium melts at about 660 °C, much lower than steel at about 1 400–1 500 °C, and it does not change colour before it melts, so it is harder to weld and needs suitable processes and skill. Mild steel is easy to weld with MMAW or oxy-acetylene, and easy to cut, drill and bend.
markingPoints: Aluminium about one third the weight of steel, with a suitable use
Mild steel stronger, stiffer and cheaper, with a suitable use
Mild steel rusts unless protected; aluminium's oxide layer protects it
Magnet sticks to mild steel, not to aluminium
Aluminium melts at a much lower heat with no colour warning, so it is harder to weld

essays.stem: Explain why steel rusts, why rust is worse near the sea in Jamaica, and describe three ways to protect steel from rust.
essays.modelAnswer: Steel rusts when the iron in it reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide, the red-brown, flaky rust. Rust is weak and falls away, so the steel gets thinner and weaker over time. Near the sea, for example in Kingston Harbour or Montego Bay, the air carries salt and is often damp. Salt water carries electric current much better than fresh water, and this speeds up the reaction, so steel on the coast rusts much faster. Steel can be protected in several ways. Painting with a primer and a top coat keeps water and air off the surface. Galvanising coats the steel with zinc, which protects it even when it is scratched, because the zinc corrodes first. Using stainless steel, which contains chromium, gives a material that resists rust. Oiling or greasing tools and keeping steel dry in the store also helps.
markingPoints: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water
Rust weakens the steel as it flakes away
Salt in damp sea air speeds up rusting
Gives three correct ways to protect steel (paint, galvanising, stainless, oil or dry storage)
Explains how at least one method protects the steel

essays.stem: A customer in Ocho Rios wants a front gate for a house near the sea. Compare mild steel, galvanised steel, stainless steel and aluminium for the job, and say which you would recommend and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Mild steel is strong, cheap and easy to cut and weld, but near the sea it will rust quickly unless it is painted well and the paint is kept up. Galvanised steel is mild steel with a zinc coating, so it lasts much longer near the sea and is still strong and fairly cheap; but the coating must be cleaned off where it is welded, the zinc fumes must be extracted, and the welds must be painted afterwards. Stainless steel resists rust very well and looks good, but it costs much more and needs more skill to weld. Aluminium is light and does not rust, but it is not as strong, dents more easily, costs more than mild steel and is harder to weld. For a seaside gate at a fair price, I would recommend galvanised steel, with the welds cleaned and painted with a zinc-rich primer and a top coat, or stainless steel if the customer can pay more.
markingPoints: Mild steel: strong, cheap, easy to weld, but rusts quickly near the sea
Galvanised steel: lasts longer; coating removed and fumes extracted for welding; welds painted
Stainless steel: best rust resistance but costly and harder to weld
Aluminium: light and rust-free but weaker, dents and is harder to weld
Makes a clear recommendation with sound reasons

essays.stem: Explain why materials must be correctly identified before they are used, and describe how a workshop can label and keep track of its materials.
essays.modelAnswer: Different metals can look alike. If the wrong material is used, the job can fail: a high-carbon bar might crack when it is welded, or mild steel used instead of stainless steel on a boat fitting will soon rust. The wrong material may also need a different process, filler or heat. To prevent mistakes, each bar, sheet and plate should be labelled when it arrives, with its material, grade and size, and the supplier's certificate should be kept on file. Many workshops paint a colour code on the ends of bars, with a chart on the wall showing what each colour means, and re-mark offcuts before they go back on the rack. Different materials are kept in separate, labelled racks, and the material used is written on the job card. If a piece has no label, it is tested or set aside and the instructor is asked.
markingPoints: Explains why: wrong material can fail or need a different process
Labels material, grade and size when it arrives
Keeps the supplier's certificates
Uses a colour code and re-marks offcuts; separate labelled racks
Records material on the job card; unlabelled pieces tested or set aside

essays.stem: Explain how the size of each common steel form is described (for example sheet, flat bar, round bar, angle and square tube), and write an example of how you would order the steel for a small gate frame.
essays.modelAnswer: Sheet and plate are described by thickness, then width and length, for example 1.2 mm × 1 220 mm × 2 440 mm sheet. Flat bar is described by width and thickness, such as 40 mm × 6 mm flat bar. Round bar is described by its diameter, for example 12 mm round bar. Angle is described by the length of each leg and the thickness, such as 40 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm angle. Square and rectangular hollow sections are described by their outside sizes and the wall thickness, such as 25 mm × 25 mm × 1.6 mm square tube. The material, such as mild steel or galvanised steel, and the length and number of lengths must also be given. For a small gate frame I might order: 4 lengths of 40 mm × 40 mm × 1.6 mm mild steel square tube, 6 m long; 2 lengths of 12 mm mild steel round bar, 6 m long; and 1 length of 40 mm × 6 mm flat bar, 6 m long.
markingPoints: Sheet and plate: thickness, width and length
Flat bar by width and thickness; round bar by diameter
Angle by leg sizes and thickness; hollow section by outside sizes and wall thickness
Says the material and the length and number of lengths must be given
Writes a complete, sensible order for the gate frame

essays.stem: Explain how materials should be stored and handled in the workshop store, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Store bars and tubes on racks off the floor, sorted by material and size and labelled, so that they stay dry and are easy to find. Store sheet flat or on edge in a rack so that it does not bend, with sharp edges protected. Keep stainless steel and aluminium apart from mild steel, and do not use the same brushes or grinding discs on them, because steel dust leaves rust spots on stainless steel and spoils aluminium welds. Keep the store dry and covered, because rain and sea air cause rust. Keep heavy items low on the racks, and keep plastics and rubber away from heat and sunlight. When handling, wear gloves against sharp edges, lift with your legs, get help or a lifting aid for heavy or long pieces, and carry long bars with a person at each end. Keep walkways clear and put offcuts back in the right rack.
markingPoints: Racks off the floor, sorted by material and size, labelled
Sheet stored flat or on edge so it does not bend
Stainless and aluminium kept apart from mild steel, with the reason
Store dry and covered; heavy items low; plastics away from heat
Safe handling: gloves, lifting with the legs, help for long or heavy pieces

practical1.title: Identifying and sorting unknown metal samples with simple tests
practical1.brief: As a group, identify a set of 10 numbered metal and plastic samples. Set up a test table and a record sheet together. Each member carries out the appearance, weight, magnet and file tests on at least two samples while the assessor watches, and records the results. Only bare samples that the magnet test shows to be ferrous are spark tested on the bench grinder, by members in turn under the assessor's eye. The group then agrees a name for each sample, sorts the samples into ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals and non-metals on a labelled board, and each member explains one result to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the record sheet is complete and the area is clean.
materials: 10 numbered samples about 100 mm long (for example mild steel, high-carbon steel, cast iron, stainless steel, galvanised steel, aluminium, copper, brass, bronze and PVC)
Magnet, file, steel rule, and a spring balance or kitchen scale
Bench grinder with its guard and eye shield, and the tool rest set close to the wheel
Record sheet with a column for each test
Board or table with three labelled areas: ferrous, non-ferrous, non-metal
photos: The samples numbered and laid out, with the blank record sheet
The magnet test on a sample
The file test on a sample
A spark test on a ferrous sample, with the member in eye protection
The samples sorted on the labelled board
checklist: Wore safety glasses throughout and a face shield at the grinder; hair and sleeves secured
Carried out the appearance, weight, magnet and file tests correctly on own samples
Recorded each result clearly on the sheet
Spark tested only a sample shown to be ferrous, using the tool rest and light pressure
Named own samples correctly, or gave a sensible reason for the name chosen
Sorted samples into the right groups and explained one result to the assessor
Left the grinder switched off and the area clean
safety: Check the grinder's guard, eye shield and tool rest gap before use; stand to one side when starting it
Spark test only bare ferrous samples: never grind aluminium, copper, brass, galvanised steel or plastic on the bench grinder
Wear safety glasses and a face shield at the grinder; keep hands clear of the wheel
Ground samples get hot: hold them with pliers and let them cool
Wear gloves for sharp cut edges, and wash your hands after handling the samples

practical2.title: Material survey and selection sheet for a fabrication job
practical2.brief: As a group, survey the materials in the Centre's steel store and offcut racks. Each member finds and measures at least three different forms of supply (for example angle, channel, flat bar, round bar, square or rectangular hollow section, sheet and plate), records the material, form and size on the survey sheet, and tags each piece. Then, as a group, choose materials for a job card the assessor gives, such as a set of burglar bars for a house in Spanish Town or a boat ladder for a fisherman in Old Harbour Bay. Fill in a material selection sheet giving each part, the material and size chosen, and the reason, and make a poster or board showing labelled samples of each form. Each member presents one choice to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the sheets and poster are finished and the store is tidy.
materials: Access to the Centre's steel store and offcut racks
Survey sheet and material selection sheet
Steel rule, tape measure, vernier caliper and a magnet
Tags or masking tape and a marker
Card or board for the poster
photos: Members in gloves and boots at the steel store
A member measuring a section with a rule or caliper
Pieces tagged with their material, form and size
The completed material selection sheet for the job
The finished poster or board of labelled samples
The store left tidy, with every piece back in its rack
checklist: Wore gloves and safety boots, and handled long or heavy pieces safely
Named the form of supply of each of own pieces correctly
Measured and recorded sizes in the right order and units (for example 40 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm angle)
Identified the material of each piece with simple checks (colour, magnet, weight)
Chose a suitable material and size for a part of the job and gave a sound reason
Took part in making the poster and presented one choice clearly
Put every piece back in the right rack and left the store tidy
safety: Wear gloves: cut ends and sheet edges are sharp
Lift with your legs, and carry long bars with a person at each end
Never climb the racks; ask for help with pieces stored high up
Keep walkways clear and put pieces back as you go
Follow the Centre's rules for working in the steel store
